title: How Games Support Mods
summary: Many of the most loved games owe much of their life to **mods**: changes and additions made by players. Games that support modding on purpose provide layers for it: replaceable data and assets, scripting, plugin APIs and official editors. This lesson surveys those layers, how mods are found and loaded in order, how conflicts arise, and the responsibilities that come with letting other people's code run inside your game.
markdown:
## Layers of modding | Layer | What modders change | Example | Risk to the game | |---|---|---|---| | **Data** | Numbers and definitions: items, monsters, levels | A `monsters.ini` with tougher trolls | Low: data is validated on load | | **Assets** | Textures, models, sounds, text | A new tile set or translation | Low | | **Scripts** | Behaviour, through an embedded language (lesson 10.08) | A new boss fight in Lua | Medium: limited by the API the game exposes | | **Plugins** | Native code (DLLs) through a plugin API | A new rendering effect or game system | High: native code can do anything the game can | | **Official tools** | Whole levels and campaigns, in the developers' editor | Map editors, mod kits | Low to medium | Delve will support the first four in this chapter: data and asset overrides (lesson 13.02), and a plugin API for DLLs (13.03, 13.04), with scripting as an extension of lesson 10.08. ## Mods as a folder with a manifest Each mod is a folder with a small description, its **manifest**: ``` mods\ tougher-trolls\ mod.ini name, version, author, which game versions it supports data\monsters.ini overrides the base game's file lantern-light\ mod.ini plugin.dll native code (lesson 13.04) textures\light.png ``` ```ini ; mod.ini name = Lantern light version = 1.2.0 author = Ada game = 1.0, 1.1 requires = tougher-trolls ``` The game reads every manifest at start-up, shows a list where players enable mods and choose their order, and refuses mods for incompatible game versions with a clear message, rather than loading them and crashing. ## Load order and conflicts When two mods change the same thing, one has to win. Games resolve this with a **load order**: mods later in the list override earlier ones, and the base game is first. ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Base game
data/monsters.ini"] --> M1["Mod 1: tougher-trolls
data/monsters.ini"] M1 --> M2["Mod 2: easy-mode
data/monsters.ini"] M2 --> R["What the game uses:
easy-mode's file wins"] ``` Whole-file replacement means the last mod's file wins completely and the earlier mod's changes vanish: a **conflict**. Smarter games **merge** at the level of individual entries, so `tougher-trolls` can change troll health and `easy-mode` change goblin damage without fighting (lesson 13.02's practice task). Dependencies (`requires`) add ordering constraints: a mod must load after the mods it builds on (lesson 13.04's practice task sorts them). ## Responsibilities Supporting mods means letting other people's work run inside your game, for your players. That brings duties: - **Stability**: a broken mod should fail clearly ("mod X failed to load: ..."), not crash the game or corrupt saves. Lesson 13.07 covers isolation. - **Safety**: native plugins can do anything, so players should only install them from sources they trust, and the game should make it obvious when native code is involved. Data and script mods are much safer, which is why many games restrict mods to them. - **Saves**: record which mods (and versions) a save was made with, and warn when loading it without them. - **Online play**: anything affecting other players must be controlled by the server, and mods that change gameplay usually belong only in single-player or in servers that opt in. Modding games you did not make is governed by their licence and community rules. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Loading every mod without checking versions > Read the manifest and refuse incompatible mods with a clear message. > [!warning] Silent conflicts > Show which mods change the same files or entries, so players can fix their load order. > [!warning] Letting mods corrupt saves > Record the mod list in each save, and warn before loading it with different mods. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? What decides which mod wins when two change the same entry? + The load order: later mods override earlier ones - The newest mod file - The largest mod > The base game is first; each mod in the list overrides what came before. ? Why are data and script mods safer than plugin DLLs? + Data is validated and scripts can only use the functions the game exposes, while native code can do anything the game can - They are smaller - They load faster > Many games limit mods to data and scripts for this reason. ? What does a mod's manifest typically contain? + Its name, version, author, the game versions it supports, and the mods it requires - Its source code - A copy of the game > The game uses it to list, order and check mods. ```
ideas:
- Write manifests for two imaginary Delve mods, one requiring the other.
- Look at how a game you play handles mods: where they live, how load order is chosen, and what happens with conflicts.
- List which parts of Delve you would expose to modders, and which you would keep closed.

cards.q: Name the layers through which a game can support mods.
cards.a: Data overrides, asset replacement, scripting, native plugins, and official editing tools.
Two mods changing the same file or entry, so that only the later one's change takes effect.

cards.q: What responsibilities come with supporting mods?
cards.a: Failing safely when a mod breaks, making native code obvious and trusted, recording mods in saves, and keeping anything that affects other players under server control.
